meta.summary: SOLAS is the principal treaty governing the structural, equipment and operational safety standards for merchant ships. It uses a framework-plus-annex structure, with technical detail updated through the 1988 tacit-acceptance amendment procedure rather than fresh treaties. For an engineer it is the parent instrument behind machinery-space fire protection, watertight subdivision and survey/certification requirements.
keyProvisions: Ch. II-1: subdivision, stability, and machinery/electrical installation standards, including bilge pumping, steering gear and emergency power.
Ch. II-2: fire protection, detection and extinction arrangements for machinery spaces and accommodation.
Ch. III: life-saving appliances and arrangements.
Ch. V: safety of navigation, including voyage planning and carriage of navigational equipment.
Ch. VI/VII: carriage of cargoes and dangerous goods, cross-referencing the IMDG, IMSBC, IBC and IGC Codes.
Ch. IX: mandatory application of the ISM Code; Ch. XI-1/XI-2: enhanced surveys and ISPS Code security.
Ch. XIV: Polar Code safety measures; Ch. XV (newer chapter): safety measures for ships carrying industrial personnel (offshore wind/energy support vessels).
meta.applicability: Applies to cargo ships of 500 GT and above and to all passenger ships on international voyages, enforced through statutory certificates.

editions.label: Consolidated Edition

versions.summary: MEPC has progressively tightened Annex VI through EEXI, CII rating and the 2023 GHG Strategy's push toward net-zero around 2050; ECA sulphur/NOx Tier III boundaries continue to expand — MEPC 84 (27 April-1 May 2026) designated a further NOx/SOx Emission Control Area covering the Norwegian Sea and Canadian Arctic (NOx Tier III from 1 March 2026 for qualifying new ships, 0.10% sulphur fuel from 1 March 2027) and a new North-East Atlantic ECA due to enter into force 1 September 2027. The biggest pending change remains the IMO Net-Zero Framework — a global fuel standard (well-to-wake greenhouse-gas fuel intensity limits) plus a GHG pricing/remedial-unit mechanism for large ships (5,000 GT+), to be inserted as a new Annex VI Chapter 5. MEPC 83 (April 2025) approved it for large oceangoing ships, but the extraordinary session called to formally adopt it in October 2025 adjourned without agreement, and MEPC 84 (April-May 2026) also closed without an adoption vote; the Committee instead set up an intersessional working group meeting in September and November 2026 to narrow differences ahead of a possible vote at MEPC 85 (late November/early December 2026) — as of mid-2026 the Framework remains approved-but-not-yet-adopted — confirm the live status before the exam.

meta.summary: MARPOL is the principal instrument controlling operational and accidental pollution from ships, structured as six technical annexes covering different pollutant types. The 1978 Protocol absorbed the 1973 parent convention after it struggled to attract ratifications, and Annex VI (air pollution/GHG) was added later by a separate 1997 Protocol. For an engineer it is the source of oily-water separator, incinerator, sludge/bilge record-keeping and emissions requirements.
keyProvisions: Annex I (1983): oil pollution prevention — machinery-space bilge discharge standards, ODMCS, Oil Record Book Part I, SOPEP.
Annex II (1983): control of noxious liquid substances carried in bulk, cargo record book, P&A manual.
Annex III (1992): prevention of pollution by harmful substances in packaged form (aligns with the IMDG Code).
Annex IV (2003): sewage pollution prevention and sewage treatment plant standards.
Annex V (1988): garbage management, discharge distances and the Garbage Record Book.
Annex VI (2005): air pollution — SOx/NOx emission limits, fuel oil sulphur caps, EEDI/EEXI and CII energy-efficiency regulations, and shipboard incinerators.
meta.applicability: Applies to all ships, with thresholds varying by annex and gross tonnage; Annexes I, II and VI carry the heaviest engine-room compliance burden for a 2nd Engineer.

meta.summary: The Load Lines Convention sets minimum freeboard and reserve-buoyancy standards so that ships are not loaded beyond a safe limit for the zone and season they trade in. The 1988 Protocol harmonised survey and certification dates with SOLAS and MARPOL and introduced the tacit-amendment procedure. For an engineer it underpins stability, watertight closing-appliance and freeing-port requirements tied to draft marks.
keyProvisions: Annex I, Ch. II: conditions of assignment of freeboard — strength/stability requirements plus freeboard-deck opening and closing-appliance provisions (hatchways, doors, ventilators, freeing ports).

Annex I, Ch. IV: special requirements for ships assigned timber freeboards.
Annex II: zones, areas and seasonal periods governing which load line applies where.
1988 Protocol: harmonised survey scheme aligning Load Line, SOLAS and MARPOL certificate renewal dates.

meta.summary: The SAR Convention created a coordinated international framework of search and rescue regions and rescue coordination centres so that survivors at sea are rescued regardless of where an incident occurs or the nationality of the ship. 2004 amendments (in force 2006): obligation to deliver rescued persons to a place of safety without delay, coordinated with the parallel SOLAS V amendments.

meta.summary: The London Convention was one of the first global treaties to control ocean dumping, originally listing prohibited and permit-controlled wastes. The 1996 Protocol, intended to eventually replace the parent Convention, reversed the approach into a 'reverse list' — dumping is prohibited for everything except a short list of substances that may be considered for a permit. It matters to engineers mainly through its overlap with MARPOL Annex V/VI on what may never be discharged or incinerated at sea.
keyProvisions: Annex I (1972 Convention): prohibited wastes (e.g., organohalogens, mercury, cadmium, persistent plastics, radioactive waste).
Annex II (1972 Convention): wastes requiring special permits.
1996 Protocol Annex 1: reverse list — only listed materials (e.g., dredged material, sewage sludge, inert geological material) may be considered for dumping permits.
1996 Protocol Art. 3: application of a precautionary approach to waste-management decisions.
Both instruments: prohibition on incineration of wastes at sea.
meta.applicability: Applies to deliberate disposal of wastes at sea from ships, aircraft and platforms in waters under the jurisdiction of parties and on the high seas.

nodes.label: LC72
nodes.title: London Convention 1972 — the black/grey list approach
nodes.summary: The original 1972 dumping treaty took a permissive approach: everything could in principle be dumped at sea unless a control applied, with a 'black list' of substances banned outright and a 'grey list' of substances that could be dumped only under a special permit, everything else needing a general permit. It defines dumping as the deliberate disposal at sea of wastes from ships, aircraft, platforms and other man-made structures.

meta.summary: The Athens Convention sets the liability regime for carriers of passengers by sea, covering death, personal injury and loss of/damage to luggage, with fault-based liability for most incidents. meta.summary: MLC 2006 is the ILO's consolidated 'fourth pillar' of international maritime regulation alongside SOLAS, MARPOL and STCW, bringing together dozens of earlier labour conventions into a single instrument covering seafarers' employment conditions, accommodation, health, welfare and social security protection. Compliance is verified through a Maritime Labour Certificate and Declaration of Maritime Labour Compliance (DMLC), inspected under a port State control regime distinct from the traditional IMO PSC MOUs.
keyProvisions: Title 1: minimum requirements for seafarers to work on a ship — minimum age, medical certification, training and recruitment/placement.
Title 2: conditions of employment — seafarers' employment agreements (SEA), wages, hours of work/rest, leave entitlement, repatriation.
Title 3: accommodation, recreational facilities, food and catering standards.
Title 4: health protection, medical care, welfare and social security protection, including shipowner liability for illness/injury.
Title 5: compliance and enforcement — flag State inspection/certification (DMLC Parts I & II) and onboard complaint procedures.
2014/2016/2018/2022 amendments: added financial security for abandonment and for shipowner liability claims, plus shore-leave and crew-change protections.

meta.summary: The ISM Code requires companies to operate a documented Safety Management System (SMS) covering the ship and shore organisation, shifting safety culture from prescriptive rule-following to proactive risk management and continuous improvement. Section 9: reports and analysis of non-conformities, accidents and hazardous occurrences.
Sections 12-13: internal audits, company verification, review and certification (DOC/SMC).

meta.summary: The LSA Code is the mandatory technical standard for the design, construction and performance of life-saving appliances and arrangements required under SOLAS Chapter III, replacing scattered convention-annex specifications with one consolidated set of performance and testing requirements. It covers everything from lifebuoys and immersion suits through lifeboats, liferafts, rescue boats and launching appliances, and is the direct technical backing behind the LSA equipment a 2nd Engineer inspects and maintains.
keyProvisions: Ch. I: General — definitions and general performance requirements applicable to all life-saving appliances.
Ch. II: Personal life-saving appliances — lifebuoys, lifejackets, immersion suits and anti-exposure suits.
Ch. III: Visual signals — rocket parachute flares, hand flares and buoyant smoke signals.
Ch. IV: Survival craft — liferafts and lifeboats, including free-fall, totally enclosed and fire-protected lifeboats.
Ch. V: Rescue boats.
Ch. VI: Launching and embarkation appliances, including davits and on-load release gear.
Ch. VII: Other life-saving appliances — line-throwing appliances and general emergency alarm/PA systems.
meta.applicability: Mandatory under SOLAS Ch. III Reg. 34 for the life-saving appliances and arrangements carried aboard SOLAS ships; the amendment procedure is set out in SOLAS Reg. III/3.10.

nodes.summary: Rescue boats largely inherit the general lifeboat requirements of section 4.4 (with an 82.5 kg seating basis) but add their own rules: 3.8-8.5 m length, capacity for at least five seated persons plus a stretcher case, a minimum 6-knot speed sustained 4 hours fully loaded, at least 2-knot towing ability for the largest liferaft aboard, inboard or outboard propulsion (including permitted petrol outboards with protected fuel systems), self-bailing, all-round visibility from the control position, and a defined standard equipment list (oars, bailer, compass, sea-anchor, painter with release device, tow line, torch, whistle, first-aid kit, rescue quoits, searchlight, radar reflector, thermal protective aids).

meta.summary: The FTP Code sets the standardized laboratory test methods used to demonstrate that construction materials, linings, furniture and fire doors meet the non-combustibility, smoke/toxicity and fire-resistance standards prescribed elsewhere in SOLAS Chapter II-2, so that 'A', 'B' and 'F' class divisions and other fire-safety products are approved on a uniform, internationally comparable basis rather than under differing national test regimes. It was originally adopted in 1996 (resolution MSC.61(67)) and comprehensively revised as the 2010 FTP Code (resolution MSC.307(88)), which is the version now referenced by SOLAS.
keyProvisions: Annex 1 (Parts 1-9 in the original 1996 structure, largely retained in the 2010 revision): fire test procedures — non-combustibility, smoke & toxicity, and fire-resistance tests for 'A', 'B' and 'F' class divisions.
Part 4: test for fire door control systems, including interpretation of results.
Parts 6-9: tests for primary deck coverings, vertically supported textiles/films, upholstered furniture and bedding components.
Annex 2: products which may be installed without further testing/approval; Annex 3: use of other fire test procedures.
Referenced throughout SOLAS Ch. II-2 as the mandatory test standard for materials used in fire-rated construction, linings and furnishings.
meta.applicability: Referenced by SOLAS Ch. II-2 as the mandatory fire test standard for construction materials, linings, furniture and fire door control systems fitted aboard SOLAS ships.

nodes.title: Scope, application and definitions
nodes.summary: Establishes that the Code is the tool Administrations and their competent authorities use to approve products against SOLAS Chapter II-2's fire-safety requirements, and that testing laboratories must use it when testing and evaluating those products. Wherever the Convention calls for something to be tested 'in accordance with the Fire Test Procedures Code', or simply requires low flame-spread/fire-resistance performance, the applicable part of Annex 1 governs. Key terms are defined, including the standard time-temperature curve a furnace must follow during a standard fire test.

nodes.title: Testing and approval procedures
nodes.summary: Requires fire tests to be run only in laboratories the Administration recognizes as independent of the product's manufacturer/vendor and operating under an audited quality-control system, with prescribed content for test reports. Products are then approved either by type approval — a certificate valid up to five years, renewable on fresh test reports, requiring the manufacturer's own audited quality system — or by one-off case-by-case approval limited to a specific ship, without a type-approval certificate.

nodes.title: Products exempt from testing, equivalents and transitional test procedures
nodes.summary: Annex 2 lists product groups that may be installed without any testing or approval at all because their fire performance is already assured by their composition. Administrations may also accept modern products tested and verified by methods not spelled out in the Code, provided they notify the Organization with a written justification. A limited period of grace lets Administrations keep using pre-existing (legacy) test procedures and acceptance criteria instead of Annex 1 while labs and industry catch up, with the applicable expiry dates fixed in Annex 3.

meta.summary: The IGF Code provides a mandatory, goal-based framework for the safe design, installation and operation of gas/low-flashpoint fuel systems, addressing the growth in LNG- and methanol-fuelled newbuildings. It sets functional requirements for fuel storage, bunkering, gas detection and machinery-space arrangements rather than fixed prescriptive rules, giving flexibility for emerging fuel technologies — a highly examinable topic for engineers on dual-fuel tonnage.
keyProvisions: Ch. 4: general requirements — risk assessment and functional requirements for gas-fuelled machinery.
Ch. 5-7: ship design/arrangement, fuel-containment system design and material/pipe design for low-flashpoint fuel systems.
Ch. 8: bunkering system design and operations, including pressure/vacuum protection.
Ch. 10-12: power generation (including gas-fuelled internal combustion engines), fire safety and explosion prevention/protection.
Ch. 17-18: operational requirements and crew training linked to STCW.
Linked to SOLAS Ch. II-1 Part G, which makes the Code mandatory for new ships using low-flashpoint fuel.
meta.applicability: Applies to new cargo ships of 500 GT and above and passenger ships using natural gas or other low-flashpoint fuel, with phased application from 1 January 2017.

validity.note: Mandatory for ships within the scope of SOLAS Chapter II-1 Part G (ships using gases or other low-flashpoint fuels) from 1 January 2017; Contracting Governments are invited (not required) to voluntarily apply the Code to cargo ships under 500 gross tonnage using such fuels, per operative paragraph 3 of resolution MSC.391(95).

nodes.title: Goal and functional requirements
nodes.summary: The Code's goal is safe, environmentally-friendly design/construction/operation of gas- or low-flashpoint-fuelled propulsion/power/other machinery; 18 functional requirements cover reliability equivalent to conventional oil-fuelled machinery, minimizing fuel-hazard probability/consequences via ventilation/detection/safety actions, avoiding unacceptable loss of power, restricting and minimizing equipment in hazardous areas, preventing unintended gas accumulation, protecting components from external damage, minimizing ignition sources, safe fuel supply/storage/bunkering without abnormal venting, suitable piping/containment/relief design, safe machinery design/operation/maintenance, arrangement preventing cross-compartment fire/explosion propagation, suitable control/alarm/monitoring/shutdown systems, fixed gas and fire detection, satisfactory commissioning/trials/maintenance, adequate technical documentation, and single-failure tolerance.

nodes.title: Ship design and arrangement
nodes.summary: Requires fuel tanks located to minimize collision/grounding damage probability, fuel containment/piping arranged so released gas vents to open air, access openings arranged to prevent gas escaping to non-designed spaces, mechanically protected piping, and machinery-space design minimizing gas-explosion probability. Sets precise fuel-tank protective-distance formulas (B/5 or 11.5m inboard from ship side; passenger-ship minimum B/10 or 0.8m from shell/aft terminal; cargo-ship minimum scaled by tank volume from 0.8m up to 2m; B/15 or 2m minimum from the bottom shell) with an alternative risk-based fCN calculation method, plus a two-machinery-space-concept framework (gas-safe machinery spaces, inherently safe under all conditions; ESD-protected machinery spaces, non-hazardous normally but with automatic emergency shutdown on abnormal gas conditions) and detailed regulations for bilge systems, drip trays, entrance/airlock arrangements, and fuel-piping location/protection.

meta.summary: The IMDG Code classifies dangerous goods carried in packaged form into UN hazard classes and prescribes packing, marking, labelling, stowage, segregation and documentation requirements so that incompatible substances are not stowed together and emergency responders know what they are dealing with. meta.summary: The IMSBC Code replaced the older recommendatory BC Code and became mandatory, covering the safe stowage and shipment of solid bulk cargoes, with particular focus on cargoes that can liquefy (Group A), possess chemical hazards (Group B), or are subject only to normal bulk-handling hazards (Group C). Engineers rely on it mainly for cargo-related fire, toxicity and stability risks — such as coal self-heating or nickel-ore liquefaction — that can affect machinery-space safety and ballasting operations.
keyProvisions: Section 4: general precautions — cargo information required from shippers before loading.
Section 7: cargoes that may liquefy (Group A) — Transportable Moisture Limit (TML) and Flow Moisture Point testing.
Section 8: cargoes possessing chemical hazards (Group B) — including self-heating, toxic-gas emission and corrosive cargoes.
Section 9: cargoes not subject to liquefaction or chemical hazard (Group C).
Individual schedules: cargo-specific hazards and stowage/segregation requirements for named cargoes (e.g., coal, nickel ore, DRI).
meta.applicability: Applies to all ships carrying solid bulk cargoes covered by the Code on international voyages.

nodes.title: General provisions
nodes.summary: Frames the whole Code: definitions and the Group A/B/C cargo classification (A may liquefy, B possesses chemical hazards, C neither), application to all SOLAS ships carrying solid bulk cargoes, the mandatory/recommendatory split (security provisions, conversion tables, references and the descriptive parts of individual schedules remain non-mandatory), how listed and unlisted cargoes are handled — unlisted cargoes needing a tripartite assessment between the load port, discharge port and flag State authorities — and the exemption/equivalence machinery.

nodes.title: Cargoes that may liquefy
nodes.summary: The Group A regime at the heart of bulk-carrier casualty prevention: fine-particled cargoes carried with moisture above their Transportable Moisture Limit can pass into a viscous fluid state, and the resulting free-surface/cargo-shift effect can capsize a ship rapidly — so such cargoes must not be accepted for loading when their moisture content exceeds the TML, unless carried in a specially constructed or fitted ship, with exposure to precipitation during loading controlled.

nodes.label: Appendix 2
nodes.title: Laboratory test procedures, associated apparatus and standards
nodes.summary: The laboratory backbone of the Group A regime: it specifies the three recognized methods for determining a cargo's transportable moisture limit — the flow table test (fine materials, determining moisture content and flow moisture point, with the TML derived from the FMP), the penetration test, and the Proctor/Fagerberg test — together with the associated apparatus and standards, plus procedures such as the trough test and self-heating test used for chemical-hazard classification; the choice among TML methods rests with local practice or the appropriate authorities.

keyProvisions: Part I-A Ch. 3: ship structure and Polar Class assignment by ice category (A, B, C).
Part I-A Ch. 6: machinery installations — cold-weather operability of engines, fuel systems and sea inlets.
Part I-A Ch. 7: fire safety/protection considerations specific to low temperature and ice conditions.
Part I-A Ch. 2: Polar Water Operational Manual (PWOM) — ship-specific operating capabilities and limitations.
Part I-A Ch. 11: voyage planning, taking into account ice, temperature and SAR-remoteness hazards.
Part I-A Ch. 12: manning and training additional to STCW for polar operations.
Part II-A: environmental provisions — restrictions on oil, NLS, sewage and garbage discharge in polar waters (MARPOL Annexes I, II, IV, V).
meta.applicability: Applies to SOLAS ships operating in the defined Arctic and Antarctic waters, mandatory since 1 January 2017 under SOLAS Ch. XIV and related MARPOL amendments.

nodes.label: I-A
nodes.title: Safety measures (mandatory)
nodes.summary: The mandatory safety half of the Code, made binding through SOLAS chapter XIV: twelve chapters running from general provisions (ship categories A/B/C by ice capability, the operational assessment, and the Polar Ship Certificate) through the Polar Water Operational Manual, structure, stability, watertight integrity, machinery, fire safety, life-saving, navigation and communication, to voyage planning and manning/training — each chapter framed as goals and functional requirements backed by prescriptive regulations, addressing the hazard chain unique to polar service: ice, icing, low temperature, darkness, remoteness and scarce SAR resources.

nodes.title: Polar water operational manual (PWOM)
nodes.summary: Requires every ship to carry a ship-specific Polar Water Operational Manual giving the master and officers the information needed to operate within the ship's assessed capabilities and limitations — procedures for normal polar operations, for managing conditions that exceed the ship's limitations, for use of icebreaker escort, and for contact with emergency response providers — so the operational-assessment output becomes a working bridge/engine-room document rather than a certificate entry; the associated ice-regime methodology (POLARIS, issued as IMO guidance) is the accepted tool for setting those ice limitations.

meta.title: Approval of I.C. Engines (Classification Note 7A)

editions.label: Migrated from RulesApp v1 flat data

versions.summary: This classification note is IRS's single consolidated reference for taking an internal combustion engine design — and its major components, including turbochargers — through type approval, and then certifying each production engine built to that approved design. It walks through the type-approval sequence (drawing/specification review, assessment of conformity of production, an agreed type-testing programme, the type test itself, and evaluation of the manufacturer's production arrangements) and the lighter, parallel engine-certification process each individual production unit goes through by reference to the approved design. Separate sections extend the same approval logic to dual-fuel/gas-fuel engines burning low-pressure natural gas, and — newly folded into this July 2024 edition — to methanol-fuelled engines, covering fuel/gas system documentation, risk analysis and additional type-testing conditions specific to those fuels. It applies to type-approval applications dated on or after 1 January 2025 and supersedes the December 2023 edition.

meta.title: Guidelines on Continuous Surveys of Machinery

editions.label: Migrated from RulesApp v1 flat data

versions.summary: Written to give owners and operators practical clarity on IRS's Continuous Survey of Machinery (CSM) scheme, this guideline expands on the bare rule text in Part 1, Chapter 2 of the Main Rules by publishing two worked lists: machinery items a Chief Engineer may open up and examine under CSM at ports where IRS is not represented (main engine running gear, turbochargers, auxiliary engines, most independently driven pumps, windlass, steering-gear pump, and — for gas carriers and refrigerated-cargo ships — the relevant compressors and cooling pumps), and items that must always go to an IRS surveyor instead (reduction gearing and clutches, boilers and pressure vessels, propellers, tailshafts, sea connections, automatic/bridge engine controls, gas and steam turbines, and engine trials). It also fixes the paperwork trail: the owner's advance notice to IRS Head Office, the Chief Engineer's signed Declaration of Examination of Surveyable Machinery Items, and the confirmatory survey an IRS (or collaborating-society) surveyor must still carry out at the next available port.

nodes.title: General Hull Structural Requirements
nodes.summary: Part 3 is the main structural strength part of the rule book, published across two volumes running to 17 chapters. Volume I (Chapters 1-9) carries the design-basis chapters — general definitions/documentation, materials and corrosion additions, structural design principles, stability, design loads, hull girder strength, hull local scantlings, finite element analysis and buckling — built on a net-scantling, direct-calculation approach. Volume II (Chapters 10-17) continues with fatigue assessment, special hull requirements (bow flare/bottom slamming, sternframes, rudder horns), openings and closing appliances, rudders, anchoring and mooring equipment, masts and rigging, hull welding, and hull inspection/workmanship/testing. Together these form the baseline hull scantling rules that ship-type-specific Part 5 requirements then build on.

meta.title: Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 — Replacement of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958

editions.label: Migrated from RulesApp v1 flat data

versions.summary: Parliament passed the Merchant Shipping Bill, 2024 on 11 August 2025 and it received Presidential assent on 18 August 2025 as the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 (Act No. 24 of 2025), restructuring and replacing the 1958 Act — compressing roughly 561 sections into about 325 sections across 16 parts. It formally renames India's maritime regulator from Director General of Shipping to Director General of Maritime Administration (DGMA), and is intended to harmonise domestic law more closely with current SOLAS, MARPOL, STCW and BWM Convention obligations while modernising seafarer-welfare and casualty-investigation provisions. The Central Government has since brought the Act into force with effect from 15 March 2026 (notification S.O. 1244(E) dated 10 March 2026), so it now supersedes the 1958 Act as the operative statute, with subordinate rules under the new Act being notified progressively through 2026. Part-by-part decomposition (the Act runs to 16 Parts) is deliberately not attempted in this repository yet - no official gazette text of the Act is held locally, and inventing Part titles/numbers without a primary source would risk exactly the kind of fabrication this repository is built to avoid. This entry stays at document level until that text is available.

relationships.note: Provides detailed engine-room/pump-room fire-prevention guidance supplementing the fixed/portable fire-fighting requirements of SOLAS Ch. II-2 Reg. 10.

meta.summary: This MSC circular consolidates, in a single document, practical engineering measures to prevent fires in engine-rooms and cargo pump-rooms, drawing together requirements and good practice scattered across SOLAS Chapter II-2 and various MSC resolutions/circulars. It is not a mandatory instrument in its own right, but it is the standard reference surveyors and ship designers use to interpret 'control of flammable oils' and 'control of ignition sources' requirements — a heavily examined 2nd Engineer topic given its direct bearing on engine-room fire risk.
keyProvisions: Part 2: installation practice — piping system design, flexible hoses, bellows expansion joints, filters/strainers and pressure/temperature gauges.

Part 3, Ch. 1: control of flammable oils — arrangement of pressurized fuel systems, spray shields on pressurized flammable-oil piping joints, and jacketed high-pressure fuel lines on internal combustion engines.
Part 3, Ch. 2: control of ignition sources — insulation of hot/high-temperature surfaces, protection of electrical equipment and identification of potential ignition sources.

Part 3, Ch. 4-5: measures against fuel-oil spillage, fuel oil isolation valves for multi-engine installations, and equipment-specific guidance for boilers, thermal oil installations, purifier rooms and oil heaters.
Part 4: equivalent control-of-flammable-materials, ignition-source and ventilation measures specific to cargo pump-rooms.
meta.applicability: Non-mandatory guidance for ship designers, owners, operators, shipbuilders, surveyors and Administrations applying SOLAS Ch. II-2 fire-safety requirements to engine-rooms and cargo pump-rooms.

nodes.title: Fire triangle and SOLAS fuel/heat/oxygen control
nodes.summary: Frames fire prevention as breaking one side of the fire triangle (heat/fuel/oxygen). Fuel control: spray shields, jacketed high-pressure fuel lines, piping location, tank sounding/venting arrangements. Heat control: insulation of high-temperature surfaces, temperature sensing for cargo/ballast/stripping pumps, oil-impervious insulation surfaces, spray protection of electrical equipment. Oxygen control: since air can't practically be excluded from machinery/pump-rooms, cargo pump-rooms must instead be mechanically ventilated at 20 air changes per hour using non-sparking suction-type fans.

Heat control: insulation of high-temperature surfaces, temperature sensing for cargo/ballast/stripping pumps, oil-impervious insulation surfaces, spray protection of electrical equipment. Oxygen control: since air can't practically be excluded from machinery/pump-rooms, cargo pump-rooms must instead be mechanically ventilated at 20 air changes per hour using non-sparking suction-type fans.

nodes.title: Flashpoint specification of oil fuels
nodes.summary: Oil fuels with a flashpoint below 60 degrees C (closed cup) are not permitted except for restricted-service ships in guaranteed-cold climates, IACS UR M24 crude-oil-as-fuel installations, and emergency generators (minimum 43 degrees C). Storage tanks must not be heated to within 10 degrees C of flashpoint, with limited exceptions for service/settling tanks meeting vent-length, temperature-sensor, flame-screen and no-machinery-space-opening conditions.

nodes.title: Control of ignition source, incl. temperature monitoring system
nodes.summary: Steam/heating media in the cargo area must not exceed 220 degrees C; lighting other than emergency lighting must be interlocked with ventilation. Temperature monitoring is required for cargo, ballast, stripping and tank-cleaning pumps driven by shafts through pump-room bulkheads (small pumps under 1 m3/h and bilge pumps may be exempted), with sensors at bulkhead shaft glands, bearings and pump casings, typically set to shut the pump down automatically at 60-80 degrees C within a 0-250 degrees C sensor range.

nodes.title: Control of ventilation, incl. gas detection systems
nodes.summary: Cargo pump-rooms need mechanical ventilation at 20 air changes per hour, vent outlets at least 3 m from ignition sources/accommodation openings, and an emergency air intake about 2 m above the lower grating for use if the normal intake floods. meta.summary: This circular sets the minimum content and presentation standard for the damage control plan and damage control booklet that SOLAS regulation II-1/19 (as amended by resolution MSC.216(82)) requires on board passenger and cargo ships, so that officers have clear, usable information on the ship's watertight subdivision to fight flooding and preserve residual stability after damage.
keyProvisions: Sec. 3: content of the damage control plan — watertight boundaries, cross-flooding system/blow-out plug locations, internal and external watertight/weathertight closing appliances and their controls, and bilge/ballast pump locations.

Sec. 4: damage control booklet — repeats the plan's information plus general instructions for controlling flooding effects (closing appliances, sounding/flooding-rate assessment, list/trim and free-surface guidance).
Sec. 5: visual guidance to the master, such as damage consequence diagrams.
Sec. 6: placement on board — permanently exhibited/available on the bridge (all ships), plus control station/safety centre (passenger ships) or cargo control room/ship's office (cargo ships).
Sec. 7: plans/booklets to be in printed form, with on-board computer software as a supplement only.

meta.summary: This joint FAL/MEPC/MSC/Legal Committee circular is the master checklist of every certificate, record book and manual an IMO instrument requires a ship to carry, cross-referenced to the specific convention/code provision that creates the requirement. It is the document a 2nd Engineer preparing for oral exams (or facing a PSC inspection) uses to confirm which record books and machinery-related certificates must physically be on board and which regulation to cite for each.
keyProvisions: Lists certificates required of all ships to which the referenced convention applies — e.g. International Tonnage Certificate (Tonnage 1969, article 7) and International Load Line Certificate (LL 1966/1988 Protocol, article 16).
Lists engine-room/pollution-prevention certificates and record books — IOPP Certificate and Oil Record Book, SOPEP, IAPP Certificate, and Ballast Water Management Certificate and Record Book.

Lists the Coating Technical File requirement for dedicated seawater ballast tanks, bulk-carrier double-side skin spaces and crude-oil-tanker cargo tanks (SOLAS Reg. II-1/3-2 and II-1/3-11, resolutions MSC.215(82)/MSC.288(87) as amended).

meta.summary: Issued after a series of fatal lifeboat drill/servicing accidents traced to on-load release hook failures, this circular gives interim design and operating guidance for Fall Preventer Devices (FPDs) — locking pins or synthetic strops/slings that provide a secondary load path if a lifeboat's on-load release hook fails or releases accidentally. FPDs are explicitly an interim risk-mitigation measure pending wider fitting of improved hook designs, not a substitute for a safe release mechanism, and are a frequently examined davit/lifeboat-safety topic.
keyProvisions: Background: traces the requirement for on-load release hooks to the 1980 Alexander Kielland platform capsize, and subsequent accidents attributed to poor maintenance, design or training of those hooks.

Sec. 2.1: locking pins — clear colour-coded operating instructions, cannot be inserted wrongly, confirmed in place before turning out and during descent, and removed (with warning procedures) before the release mechanism is activated.

Sec. 2.2: strops or slings — synthetic only (wires/chains do not absorb shock loads), functional-tested, certified to a safety factor of at least 6 on full loaded lifeboat weight, inspected every six months, and marked with date of entry into service.
Both FPD types: must be removable quickly and safely by crew inside the craft once waterborne, and re-secured before the lifeboat is hoisted clear of the water.
meta.applicability: Interim guidance for masters, owners and Administrations approving the use of FPDs on existing on-load release hook systems for lifeboats and rescue boats.

nodes.title: Background
nodes.summary: Traces the requirement for on-load release hooks to the March 1980 capsize of the Alexander Kielland platform, then explains that subsequent lifeboat drill and servicing accidents were traced to poorly maintained, poorly designed or poorly understood hooks that can spring open under the lifeboat's own weight even with their built-in safety interlocks. An FPD is introduced as a secondary load path for when the hook or its release gear fails or fires accidentally — explicitly not a substitute for a safe release mechanism.

meta.summary: The 2023 SOLAS amendments touching four chapters: Chapter II-1 adds a wholly new Regulation 3-13 covering ship's cranes, stores cranes, and anchor handling winches (classification-society or equivalent design/construction standards, load testing, periodic examination); Chapter II-2 restricts fire-extinguishing media containing PFOS on ships built on/after 1 January 2026; Chapter V adds bulk carrier/containership definitions and requires an electronic inclinometer on containerships and bulk carriers of 3,000 GT+ built on/after 1 January 2026; and Chapter XIV extends Polar Code Part I-A applicability (machinery installations, voyage planning) to fishing vessels, non-trading pleasure yachts, and smaller cargo ships not previously covered. Consequential amendments update several statutory certificate forms (immersion suit terminology, a new "Containership" ship-type entry, an electronic inclinometer equipment-record entry).

II-1/3-13 applies to ships fitted with lifting appliances/anchor handling winches; the Chapter II-2 PFOS restriction applies to ships constructed on/after 1 January 2026; the Chapter V electronic inclinometer requirement applies to containerships and bulk carriers of 3,000 GT and upwards constructed on/after 1 January 2026; the Chapter XIV expansion applies to fishing vessels ≥24m LOA, non-trading pleasure yachts ≥300GT, and cargo ships 300-500GT operating in polar waters. All amendments entered into force 1 January 2026.

nodes.title: Lifting appliances and anchor handling winches (new regulation)
nodes.summary: A wholly new regulation, inserted in Part A-1 after Reg. 3-12: applies to lifting appliances, anchor handling winches, and their loose gear (with express carve-outs for MODU-certified lifting appliances, offshore construction ship equipment meeting acceptable standards, integrated hatch-cover-opening machinery, and LSA-Code launching appliances). Requires equipment installed on/after 1 January 2026 to be designed/constructed/installed to a recognized classification society's requirements or an equivalent Administration-accepted standard, load tested and thoroughly examined before first use and after major repairs, permanently marked with safe working load, and — for anchor handling winches — designed/tested to Organization-developed Guidelines. Equipment installed before that date must be brought up to the testing/examination/marking requirements by the first renewal survey on or after 1 January 2026. All such equipment, regardless of installation date, must be operationally tested, examined, inspected, operated and maintained per the Guidelines; a malfunction does not by itself render the ship unseaworthy provided the master has planned the voyage around it.

nodes.title: Exceptions and exemptions
nodes.summary: Excludes emissions necessary for safety/life-saving and (subject to conditions) accidental damage-related emissions; allows Administrations to exempt ships from specific provisions for emission-reduction-technology research trials (capped at 18 months, renewable, or up to 5 years for larger engines with periodic review); exempts emissions directly arising from seabed mineral exploration/exploitation; and — the resolution's narrower, previously over-emphasized clause — lets the Administration exempt a qualifying unmanned, non-self-propelled (UNSP) barge from Reg. 5.1/6.1 survey and certification requirements via an International Air Pollution Prevention Exemption Certificate for UNSP Barges, valid up to 5 years, following a confirmatory survey.

nodes.title: Duration and validity of Certificates and Statements of Compliance
nodes.summary: IAPP Certificates run up to 5 years with detailed renewal/extension/grace-period rules; the International Energy Efficiency Certificate is valid for the ship's life (voided by withdrawal from service, major conversion, flag transfer without re-verification, or unapproved equipment changes); fuel-oil/CII Statements of Compliance are valid for the issuing calendar year plus a defined carry-over period into the next, and must be retained on board for at least 5 years.

nodes.summary: Sets the Annex's original air-pollution-control regime: ozone-depleting substances, NOx Tier I/II/III engine emission limits and Emission Control Areas, SOx/fuel-sulphur limits (0.50% m/m globally, 0.10% m/m in Emission Control Areas), volatile organic compounds from tankers, shipboard incineration, reception facilities, and fuel oil availability/quality (including bunker delivery notes and sampling).

nodes.title: Ozone-depleting substances
nodes.summary: Prohibits deliberate emissions of ozone-depleting substances (minimal recapture/recycling releases excepted); bans new installations containing such substances (other than HCFCs) on ships built on/after 19 May 2005, and HCFC-containing installations on ships built on/after 1 January 2020; requires an equipment list and, for rechargeable systems, an ozone-depleting-substances record book logging recharges, repairs, discharges, and supply.

nodes.title: Fuel oil availability and quality
nodes.summary: Parties must promote compliant fuel-oil availability; a non-compliant ship may present evidence of a genuine, documented attempt to obtain compliant fuel without being required to deviate/delay its voyage. Fuel oil must be petroleum-refining-derived hydrocarbon blends free of inorganic acid and harmful additives (or, for non-petroleum-derived fuels, meet equivalent sulphur/NOx/safety criteria); requires a bunker delivery note (retained 3 years) and a sealed representative sample (retained 12 months) per delivery, with fuel suppliers subject to Party oversight and reporting for non-compliant deliveries.

nodes.title: Regulations on the carbon intensity of international shipping
nodes.summary: The heart of the 2021 revision: applies to ships of 400 GT and above (with defined exclusions for domestic-only voyages, non-mechanically-propelled craft, platforms, and Polar Code category A ships); sets the goal of reducing shipping's carbon intensity toward the Initial IMO GHG Strategy's ambition via technical (EEDI/EEXI, Reg. 22-25) and operational (SEEMP/data collection/CII, Reg. 26-28) requirements, plus technical cooperation provisions (Reg. 29).

meta.summary: The HSSC Survey Guidelines translate the harmonized survey and certification scheme introduced by the 1988 SOLAS and Load Line Protocols into a single practical reference, defining the types of survey (initial, annual, intermediate, periodical, renewal, additional) and mapping each to the specific regulation of SOLAS, the Load Line Convention, MARPOL, the BWM Convention and the IBC/IGC/BCH Codes that requires it. nodes.title: Introduction
nodes.summary: States that these 2023 Guidelines revoke the 2021 edition and take account of the harmonized survey/certification scheme across SOLAS 74/88, the Load Line Convention 66/88, MARPOL, the BWM Convention, the IBC/IGC/BCH Codes and the Polar Code. It summarises the harmonized system's core mechanics: a one-year standard survey interval (except MARPOL Annex IV, which uses only initial and renewal surveys), a renewal survey completed up to three months early with no loss of validity, a six-month time window for annual/intermediate/periodical surveys, a maximum five-year certificate validity for cargo ships (twelve months for the Passenger Ship Safety Certificate), a bounded extension system for ships unable to reach a survey port, the flexible two-inspections-per-five-years scheme for the outside of a cargo ship's bottom, and the option of a single combined Cargo Ship Safety Certificate in place of separate Equipment/Construction/Radio certificates.

nodes.summary: Explains that the Guidelines are a general framework, not necessarily applicable to every ship type/size; that they should also be applied, as appropriate, to drilling rigs/platforms under MARPOL Annex I Reg. 39 and Annex VI Reg. 5; that a Cargo Ship Safety Certificate may substitute for the separate Equipment/Construction/Radio certificates, with its surveys following the certificates it replaces; and sets out the certificate-letter/survey-type-letter abbreviation scheme (e.g. (E) equipment, (C) construction, (R) radio, (L) load line, (O) oil pollution, (N) NLS, (S) sewage, (A) air pollution, (D)/(G) chemical/gas fitness, (P) passenger ship, (W) polar ship, (B) ballast water, (T) industrial personnel; combined with (I)/(A)/(In)/(P)/(R)/(B)/(Ad) for survey type) used as a shorthand prefix throughout Annexes 1-5.

nodes.title: Description of the various types of survey
nodes.summary: Gives the detailed frequency and scope of each survey type: initial surveys (before entry into service, covering plan examination, physical inspection, and a documentation check); annual surveys (within 3 months either side of the anniversary date, a certificate/visual examination confirming maintained condition and no unapproved modifications); intermediate surveys (within 3 months either side of the 2nd or 3rd anniversary date, replacing an annual survey); periodical surveys (similarly windowed, for equipment-focused certificates); renewal surveys (before certificate expiry, may commence at the 4th annual survey for cargo ship safety construction); inspection of the outside of the ship's bottom (minimum two inspections per 5-year certificate period, interval capped at 36 months, normally in dry dock — bulk carriers/oil tankers of 15+ years must be in dry dock); additional surveys (after an accident, important repair, or BWMS retrofit); and the completion-of-survey consequences (a condition/deficiency-notice regime) when deficiencies exist that do not endanger the ship but cannot be immediately rectified.

nodes.title: Amplification of terms and conditions
nodes.summary: Clarifies 15 recurring terms/mechanisms across the harmonized instruments: the meaning of "related items" (only inspectable in dry dock/in-water bottom examination); extending a short-duration certificate to a full five years while preserving the equivalent survey pattern; extending the interval between bottom inspections (36-month cap still applies); the 1,000-mile definition of "short voyage"; "special circumstances" allowing a renewal survey to date from actual completion rather than the prior certificate's expiry (e.g. after lay-up); revalidation after a lapsed survey (the certificate is invalid until the missed survey is carried out, with its rigor reflecting how long it lapsed); the meaning of "any five-year period"; procedure when a ship transfers flag (new Administration withholds certificates until satisfied of proper maintenance, old Administration forwards prior certificates/survey records); recommended conditions for extending a certificate's validity when the ship is away from the issuing port at expiry; inspection of a passenger ship's bottom; survey of radio installations; survey of the automatic identification system (AIS); surveys for ships intended to operate in polar waters; surveys for ships carrying more than 12 industrial personnel; and provision for remote surveys.

versions.summary: DG Shipping circulated a notice (Ref. SL RUL-LLMC-3(11)/12) inviting stakeholder comments, by 9 February 2016, on a draft Merchant Shipping (Limitation of Liability for Maritime Claims) Amendment Rules, 2016. The draft was intended to revise Rule 3 of the then-current Merchant Shipping (Limitation of Liability for Maritime Claims) Rules, 2015 (notified vide G.S.R. 93(E) dated 16 December 2015) so that India's limitation figures track the increased tonnage-based limits adopted for the 1996 LLMC Protocol by IMO Legal Committee Resolution LEG.5(99) (adopted 19 April 2012), which entered into force by tacit acceptance on 8 May 2015 under Article 8(4) of the Protocol. The draft raised, among other figures, the loss-of-life/personal-injury limitation amounts from 2 million to 3.02 million Units of Account and the property-claim limitation amounts from 1 million to 1.51 million Units of Account, mirroring the LEG.5(99) revisions to Article 3 of the 1996 Protocol. The extracted text available does not confirm whether or when the amendment rules were subsequently finalised and notified.

engineeringObjects.title: Fire Main and Fire Pump System
engineeringObjects.description: The ship's permanent, pressurized water-fighting backbone: a piping main run to hydrants throughout the vessel, supplied by two or more independently driven fire pumps sized and numbered by ship type and tonnage, plus a segregated emergency fire pump whose entire purpose is to keep water available at the hydrants even if a fire in the main machinery space takes out every other pump on board. The system's defining engineering problem is not the pump or the pipe individually, but the segregation logic connecting them: isolating valves split the fire main so the machinery-space section can be shut down without losing the rest of the ship, and the emergency pump's space, suction, and power source must sit outside the machinery space specifically so the one fire most likely to disable the main pumps cannot disable this one too.

extensions.text: Regulation 10 reads as a flat list of requirements, but it is really a layered defense, and the layers matter for understanding why any one paragraph exists. The fixed water-based system (2: fire main, pumps, hydrants, hoses) is the baseline every ship carries regardless of type. Portable extinguishers (3) exist for first response, before the fixed system is even needed. The additional fixed systems layered on top -- gas flooding (4), water-spray/mist (5), sprinkler/detection/alarm (7), deck foam (8) -- are not redundant with the fire main; they target specific high-consequence spaces (Category A machinery spaces, cargo holds, tanker decks) where a fire main and hose alone would be too slow or too dangerous to approach with. The regulation's real engineering center of gravity is paragraph 2.2's fire pump and emergency fire pump requirement, because it is the one paragraph explicitly designed around a failure scenario rather than a steady-state specification: the emergency pump, its space, its suction, and its power source all have to sit outside the machinery space specifically so that the fire most likely to take out the main pumps -- a machinery-space fire -- cannot also take out the ship's ability to fight it. Every other detailed requirement in 2.1 (isolating valves splitting the fire main so the machinery-space section can be shut down without losing the rest of the ship) exists to serve that same single idea: the system must survive the exact scenario it exists to fight.

extensions.text: Working points a Chief Engineer actually needs, not just the regulation number. Pump siting: the pump and its suction must work at the lightest service draft the ship will realistically see, accounting for list, trim, roll, pitch, and the slow internal corrosion buildup in the suction pipe over the ship's life -- a pump that primes fine on commissioning can lose that margin years later purely from pipe fouling. A 'throw-over' sea suction is only acceptable for the second fire pump on older vessels (built before 16 December 1998 under the old MCA LY1 Code) -- not something to expect or specify on a modern build. If the pump sits more than 2 m above the lightest service draft, air-extraction priming should normally be fitted; where a positive-displacement pump is used instead, the recommended suction head limit is 4.5 m. IACS Unified Interpretation SC164 recommends the emergency fire pump specifically be self-priming where priming would otherwise be marginal. Hose/nozzle sizing is a paired decision, not two independent ones: nozzle size is picked from the pressure/discharge table against the smallest fire pump the regulations allow, and standard hose bore is 64 mm unlined, though 45 mm lined hose has been shown to match a 64 mm unlined hose's throughput while being easier to handle -- a real, evidenced tradeoff worth knowing when a smaller-diameter hose shows up in machinery spaces. One detail worth remembering precisely because it is easy to get backwards: the ballast condition of a ship entering or leaving dry dock is explicitly NOT to be treated as a service condition when assessing whether the fire pump will prime and deliver at the lightest draft the ship will see (MSC/Circ.847) -- dry-docking is not the scenario this requirement is protecting against.

extensions.text: What a surveyor actually checks at initial survey, organized by system component -- useful as a pre-survey self-check before the surveyor arrives. Fire main: correct materials and approved-type joints fitted; hydrostatic pressure test completed (2.0x max working pressure where that pressure exceeds 7 bar at the pump discharge, 1.5x where it is below 7 bar); non-return valves fitted and accessible; isolation valves fitted, labelled, and demonstrated working; any insulated fire-main sections routed through the machinery space confirmed satisfactory. Hydrants and hoses: correct lengths and diameters supplied for each space; couplings correctly bound to hose ends; nozzle size and type correct; the required number of jets, of the required length, actually deliverable to the spaces they are meant to cover; hoses demonstrably controllable by one person at the working pressure. Fire pumps: remote and automatic start functions tested; pumps run efficiently and prime correctly; correct hydrant pressure delivered at the highest hydrant on the ship (the worst case, since pressure is lowest there); any additional non-designated pumps connected to the fire main operate satisfactorily. Emergency fire pump specifically: separation from the main fire pumps' space confirmed satisfactory; remote power sources confirmed separated from the machinery spaces; heating arrangements for a diesel-driven unit in an unheated space confirmed adequate; starting system tested to the actual standard (at least six starts in thirty minutes, at least two of those in the first ten minutes); fuel supply confirmed adequate, both the immediate onboard supply and any required reserve; pump confirmed to run efficiently, prime correctly, and deliver the correct hydrant pressure.

extensions.text: What changes between initial survey and re-survey, and what actually degrades in service rather than just needing a one-time check. Re-survey re-confirms most of the initial-survey items (isolation valve accessibility, insulated machinery-space sections, hose condition, coupling security, nozzle condition, hydrant accessibility, pump start/prime/pressure performance) but adds a leak test of the fire main at maximum service pressure -- a check that only makes sense once the system has had time in service to develop leaks. Two specific, evidenced degradation mechanisms are worth tracking on their own maintenance schedule rather than folding into a generic 'inspect fire system' task: internal corrosion progressively reduces the bore of hydrant standpipes and valves below their as-built minimum (64 mm for galvanised steel, 50 mm for copper alloy), which quietly degrades delivered flow long before the pipe would fail outright -- this is a slow, cumulative loss of margin, not a sudden fault, and is exactly the kind of thing an inspection checklist alone will miss unless bore is actually measured periodically rather than just checked for gross damage. Second, where the emergency fire pump is battery-started, the batteries need active maintenance, not passive storage: they must be kept on trickle charge (with monitored visual/audible fault alarming if only one set is fitted) and stowed away from low temperatures that would reduce their output -- a battery bank that looks fine sitting in a cold space can fail the required six-starts-in-thirty-minutes test precisely when it is needed. Freezing-prone piping runs need periodic confirmation that drainage arrangements still work, not just that they were fitted correctly at build.

extensions.text: Concrete ways this system fails, each traceable to a specific evidenced cause rather than a generic 'pump breaks' statement. (1) Both main fire pumps disabled by a single fire: if the two main pumps, their sea suctions, and their fuel/power sources are not separated by at least A0 divisions, a fire in one compartment can take out both -- this is precisely the condition that makes an emergency fire pump mandatory rather than optional (IACS UI SC162), and the same logic applies if one main pump's compartment has more than one bulkhead or deck boundary adjacent to the other's. (2) Emergency pump fails to prime or deliver when actually needed despite passing its periodic start test: priming margin degrades gradually from internal corrosion in the suction pipe and from the pump sitting too high above the lightest realistic service draft; a start test that only checks 'does it start' without also checking delivered pressure at the highest hydrant can miss this. (3) Emergency pump starting system fails cold: diesel-driven units without electric heating of cooling water/lubricating oil in an unheated space, or battery banks not kept on trickle charge or exposed to low stowage temperatures, can fail to achieve the required six-starts-in-thirty-minutes even though the pump itself is mechanically sound. (4) Hose failure under pressure: incorrect diameter/lining selection can cause a hose to 'nip' or collapse when led around the ship, most likely to surface exactly when the hose is actually run out during a fire rather than during a static inspection. (5) Ship-wide loss of fire-main pressure from a single machinery-space fire: if isolating valves are not correctly positioned outside the machinery space per 2.1, shutting down the machinery-space section to fight a fire there also cuts off hydrants elsewhere on the ship -- the isolating-valve requirement exists specifically to prevent this, and a valve installed inside the space it is meant to isolate defeats the purpose while still technically being 'a valve'.

extensions.text: Regulation 10's current numbering and structure do not descend directly from the 1974 original. SOLAS Chapter II-2 was completely revised by IMO in December 2000, applicable from 1 July 2002 -- the current Regulation 10 is a product of that rewrite, not a lightly-amended version of the 1974 text. Earlier, the 1996 amendments (entered into force 1998) had already revised Chapter II-2's general introduction and Parts B/C/D. Most recently and specifically to Regulation 10: IMO Resolution MSC.409(97) amended SOLAS II-2/1 and II-2/10 to waive the approved foam-type extinguisher requirement (minimum 135 L capacity) for boilers already protected by a fixed water-based local-application fire-extinguishing system, applicable to all ships on or after 1 January 2020. Beyond textual amendments, a substantial body of IMO and IACS Unified Interpretations refines how specific sub-paragraphs are to be applied without changing Regulation 10's numbered text itself -- these are interpretive guidance, not amendments, and should not be confused with one another when tracking what actually changed the regulation versus what merely clarified it: MSC/Circ.847 (dry-docking ballast condition), MSC/Circ.1120 (multiple starting-arrangement and isolating-valve interpretations), MSC.1/Circ.1314 (FSS Code Ch.12 emergency pump capacity interpretation), MSC.1/Circ.1388 (emergency pump suction-head interpretation for cargo ships built on/after 1 January 2012), and IACS Unified Interpretations SC114, SC121, SC146, SC162, SC164, SC165. No amendment to Regulation 10 beyond MSC.409(97) (2020) was found in this research pass; this absence is a checked finding as of 2026-07-25, not an unchecked assumption -- it should be re-verified before being relied on much further past this date.

extensions.text: Structured decision rule for reasoning about emergency fire pump compliance, distilled specifically for downstream reasoning rather than as free-text explanation. To assess whether an emergency fire pump arrangement satisfies Reg. 10.2.2 as currently understood from evidence gathered in this pass, check in order: (1) CAPACITY -- is it at least 40% of the total required fire pump capacity, and in any case at least 25 m3/h? Below either threshold, non-compliant regardless of other factors. (2) LOCATION -- is the pump space non-contiguous with the boundaries of any Category A machinery space, with no direct access between them? If access is unavoidable, is it via a self-closing airlock with the machinery-space-side door at A-60 standard? (3) STARTING -- can the arrangement achieve at least six starts in thirty minutes, with at least two of those in the first ten minutes, using a starting source independent of the machinery spaces? (4) FUEL/POWER INDEPENDENCE -- do the pump's sea suction, power source, and (where diesel-driven) fuel supply avoid routing through or depending on the machinery space containing the main fire pumps? A single 'no' on any of these four checks is sufficient to flag the arrangement for engineering review -- they are independent requirements, not a weighted score, because each one maps to a distinct failure scenario documented in this node's failure-modes record. This rule reflects only what was verified in this authoring pass (2026-07-25) and should be re-validated against the current regulation text before being relied on for an actual compliance determination.

extensions.text: The system SOLAS II-1/29 regulates is not one machine but a chain, and each link is separately regulated. Main steering gear: the power unit(s) and actuator that move the rudder stock in normal operation -- typically a rotary vane or ram-type hydraulic actuator on modern tonnage. Auxiliary steering gear: an independent second means of moving the rudder, required specifically so a single failure cannot remove steering capability entirely -- this is the regulation's central engineering idea, not an afterthought. Rudder stock and tiller/quadrant: the mechanical link between actuator and rudder, sized against the 230 mm power-operation threshold. Hydraulic power units and piping: pumps, reservoirs, and the isolating valves Reg. 29.14 requires on large tankers specifically so a single hydraulic-line failure doesn't disable the whole system. Control system: telemotor or electric order-transmission from bridge to steering gear, including the local/emergency control position required in the steering gear compartment itself. Rudder angle indicator: independent of the control system, so the actual rudder position remains known even if control is lost. Steering gear compartment: the physical space housing all of this, itself subject to fire-protection and access requirements shared with other machinery-space regulation.

extensions.text: Steering gear is the one system on a ship where SOLAS regulates around a single design idea rather than a list of specifications: no single failure may remove the ability to steer. Everything else in Regulation 29 -- the auxiliary gear requirement, the hydraulic isolation valves on large tankers, the independent rudder angle indicator, the separate control position in the steering gear compartment -- exists to serve that one idea, not as a checklist of unrelated features. This matters for how the regulation should actually be read: a requirement that looks like an isolated technical detail (why does the auxiliary gear need its own 60-second performance standard, distinct from the main gear's 28 seconds?) usually traces back to the same single-failure logic once you ask what specific failure it's defending against. The 230 mm power-operation threshold exists because below that stock diameter, manual steering genuinely remains a viable auxiliary means -- above it, physical human force cannot reliably move the rudder in the time SOLAS requires, so power becomes mandatory rather than merely convenient.

extensions.text: Working points beyond the bare regulation numbers. The changeover to emergency/local steering is a drill, not a document -- SOLAS V/26 requires it demonstrated, and the practical sequence matters: confirm the bridge team is aware control is transferring before disconnecting remote control (Reg. 29.8.2 requires this be operable by a single person without tools, which is a deliberate design choice -- whoever is in the steering gear compartment during an actual casualty will not have time to search for a spanner), then verify rudder response to helm orders relayed by the required bridge-to-steering-gear communication link before declaring the changeover complete. The block diagram showing system configuration and changeover steps must be posted both on the bridge and in the steering gear compartment -- not filed in a manual -- because the whole point is that whoever is physically present at either end during a casualty can follow it without having read it in advance. Recording date and time of every test, check, and drill is not paperwork for its own sake: it is the evidence a PSC officer or auditor uses to confirm the 3-monthly drill interval and 12-hour pre-departure check are actually happening, not just documented as a policy.

extensions.text: SOLAS V/26's own testing regime, which is also what a surveyor or auditor actually checks. Within 12 hours before departure: main steering gear operation; auxiliary steering gear operation; remote steering gear control systems; steering position indicator on the navigating bridge relative to actual rudder position; emergency power supply to the steering gear; the rudder angle indicator itself, confirmed against actual rudder position, not just that it moves; power failure alarms for the remote control system; power unit failure alarms; and the automatic isolating arrangements required by Reg. 29.14 on qualifying tankers. Full rudder movement is verified against each system's own required performance, not a generic sweep. Beyond the pre-departure check: emergency steering drills at intervals not exceeding three months (SOLAS V/26.4) -- a surveyor checking compliance will ask for the dated drill log, not just confirm a procedure exists. All ship's officers concerned with steering gear operation or maintenance are expected to be familiar with changeover procedures specifically -- an officer who can describe the regulation but not perform the changeover has not actually met the intent of this requirement.

extensions.text: The most evidenced, and most counter-intuitive, maintenance point: hydraulic steering gear failures that present as mechanical faults are frequently actually hydraulic fluid contamination -- water ingress, metal particles from internal wear, or simply degraded oil -- and this can prevent proper operation even when every mechanical component is sound. A maintenance regime that only inspects pumps, valves, and linkages while treating fluid condition as a secondary, infrequent check is addressing the less likely cause first. Seal integrity is the specific, evidenced highest-risk item: oil leaking through seals to the surroundings has been identified as the single most dangerous failure event in steering gear risk analysis, both because it is a genuine single point of failure and because a slow leak is easy to under-prioritise against more visible defects until capacity is already compromised. For tankers of 10,000 GT and above specifically, Reg. 29.14's isolation valves are only as good as their own maintenance -- an isolation valve that has seized in the open position provides none of the single-failure protection the regulation exists to guarantee, and this is not something a routine visual check reliably catches without actually exercising the valve.

extensions.text: Three documented failure categories, not a single generic 'steering gear failure': hydraulic power failure (the actuator loses the pressure needed to move the rudder -- pump failure, contaminated fluid, or a leaking seal, per this system's own maintenance-guidance record), rudder failure (a mechanical failure downstream of the actuator -- stock, tiller, or the rudder itself), and control failure (the order-transmission chain from bridge to actuator fails even though the actuator itself remains capable -- exactly the scenario the independent auxiliary control position in the steering gear compartment exists to route around). These three categories point to different corrective actions, which is why distinguishing them during an actual casualty matters more than recognising 'steering has failed' -- a control failure is resolved by changing over to local control per SOLAS V/26's drilled procedure; a hydraulic power failure is not. A documented illustrative case (MIW Written Answers, WA3-LIEN1.html -- see MIW Resources) traces exactly this chain: a catastrophic hydraulic lock in a rotary vane steering gear stuck the rudder hard-a-port during a port approach, with no time available to complete an emergency changeover before the vessel struck a pier -- illustrating why the drilled changeover time itself, not just its existence, is operationally significant.

extensions.text: Structured decision rule for reasoning about steering gear compliance, distilled from this node's other records rather than independently authored. To assess whether a steering gear arrangement satisfies the regime as currently understood from evidence gathered in this pass, check in order: (1) DUAL CAPABILITY -- does the ship have both main and auxiliary steering gear, arranged so a failure of one cannot render the other inoperative? A single-gear arrangement fails regardless of any other factor. (2) PERFORMANCE -- does main gear achieve 35 degrees to 30 degrees opposite side within 28 seconds at max service speed/deepest draught, and auxiliary gear 15 degrees to 15 degrees within 60 seconds at half speed or 7 knots? (3) POWER OPERATION THRESHOLD -- if rudder stock diameter exceeds 230 mm, is power operation actually fitted, not just planned? (4) TANKER ISOLATION -- for tankers of 10,000 GT and above, are hydraulic isolation valves fitted and demonstrably functional, not merely present? (5) TESTING DISCIPLINE -- is the full SOLAS V/26 nine-point pre-departure check actually logged within the 12-hour window, and are 3-monthly emergency drills dated and recorded? A single 'no' on any of these five is sufficient to flag the arrangement for engineering review -- they map to independent failure scenarios documented in this node's failure-modes and maintenance-guidance records, not a weighted score. This rule reflects only what was verified in this authoring pass (2026-07-25) and should be re-validated against the current regulation text before being relied on for an actual compliance determination.

extensions.text: The emergency source of electrical power regulated by SOLAS II-1/42 is a self-contained plant, not just a spare engine. Emergency generator set: a diesel prime mover and alternator, sized to carry the full 36-hour (passenger) or 18-hour (cargo) load schedule alone, self-contained and independent of the main machinery space's fuel, cooling and starting services -- a fire or flood that disables the main plant must not be able to disable this one too. Starting arrangements: the prime mover must be capable of automatic self-starting from cold (down to 0 degrees C ambient) without any external electrical supply, typically via dedicated starting batteries or a compressed-air/hydraulic accumulator kept charged independently of the main plant, per SOLAS II-1/41.5's dead-ship starting principle extended to the emergency set. Transitional source of emergency power: a battery bank sized to bridge the gap between main power loss and the emergency generator actually coming onload, so essential lighting and communications do not go dark even for the 45 seconds SOLAS II-1/42.3 allows the generator to start and connect. Emergency switchboard and emergency lighting switchboard: physically separate from the main switchboard, positioned outside the main machinery space and its associated casings so the same casualty cannot reach both. Load schedule wiring: dedicated feeders to navigation lights, GMDSS radio installations, internal emergency communications, fire detection and alarm systems, and the specific consumers -- fire pump, sprinkler pump, emergency bilge pump, steering gear -- SOLAS II-1/42.2 names as essential safety services.

extensions.text: SOLAS II-1/42 sits downstream of II-1/41: Reg 41 requires the main electrical power source to be resilient (at least two generating sets, either capable of carrying the essential load alone) precisely so the emergency source is a true last line of defence rather than the everyday backup. The 36-hour figure for passenger ships versus 18 hours for cargo ships is not an arbitrary safety margin -- it is sized against the realistic time to organise assistance or abandon ship for each ship type, which is also why the consumer list (navigation lights, GMDSS, fire pumps, steering gear, internal communications) is deliberately the minimum needed to fight a casualty and coordinate evacuation, not the ship's full electrical load. The 45-second automatic start-and-connect requirement in Reg 42.3 exists because the transitional battery source bridging that gap is only sized for short-duration essential loads (emergency lighting, navigation lights, alarms) -- a slow-starting generator would leave heavier loads like the fire pump and steering gear unpowered for an unacceptable period. The 22.5-degree list / 10-degree trim operability requirement in Reg 42.7 reflects that the emergency source must still function in exactly the damaged-stability condition most likely to have caused the main power loss in the first place -- a generator that only works upright is of little use after the casualty that actually necessitates it. One repository-structural note for transparency: this Engineering Object's own description references an '18-hour requirement... per Reg 43' for cargo ships, but SOLAS II-1/43 (the separate cargo-ship regulation paralleling Reg 42) does not yet exist as its own node in this repository's SOLAS tree -- the cargo-ship figure is currently only captured as a value inside SOLAS-II1-42-422's paragraph text. This is a repository content-completeness gap, not an engineering-intelligence error, and is out of scope for this authoring pass; it belongs to the separate Official Content structural completion work.

extensions.text: Testing discipline for the emergency generator follows a three-tier cadence in real shipboard practice, escalating in scope: weekly, an unloaded (no-load) automatic start test is run, usually from the bridge or engine control room, confirming the set starts and reaches rated speed/voltage/frequency within the window without actually transferring the emergency bus onto it. Monthly, a test goes further and includes the automatic changeover -- simulating a main power failure (or using the test position provided for this) so the emergency switchboard genuinely transfers onto the generator, confirming the full automatic sequence Reg 42.3 requires, not just that the engine turns over. Quarterly (and always as part of the annual survey), a full blackout / dead-ship test is run under load, briefly de-energising the main switchboard entirely to prove the complete chain works exactly as it would in a real casualty: automatic start, connection within 45 seconds, and essential consumers actually picking up power. Between these scheduled tests, engineers should log start time on every test (not just pass/fail) -- a set that still starts but creeping past 30-35 seconds is an early warning of battery or starter-motor degradation well before it fails the 45-second limit outright.

extensions.text: One survey-scope fact worth knowing before an inspection, not just during one: the emergency generator is explicitly excluded from Continuous Machinery Survey (CMS) delegation to the crew/chief engineer -- it always requires direct attendance and sign-off by the class surveyor, unlike many other machinery items that can be surveyed on a rolling CMS basis. A surveyor verifying compliance with Reg 42 in practice checks, in order: (1) automatic start and 45-second connection, witnessed live, with the actual elapsed time timed and logged, not just a pass/fail tick; (2) load test under the full essential-consumer schedule (or a documented equivalent), confirming rated voltage and frequency are held under load, not just at no-load; (3) list/trim capability records -- since a live 22.5-degree list test is impractical at a berth, this is typically verified by design documentation and prime-mover/lubrication-system certification rather than a physical inclining test of the running set; (4) transitional battery source capacity and charge state, since a healthy generator with a failed transitional battery still leaves a real gap in coverage during the start window; (5) physical separation of the emergency switchboard and its cabling routes from the main machinery space, confirming the installation still matches the as-built drawings. A generator that starts fine on a scheduled test but was never actually surveyed under full load is a common finding -- weekly/monthly crew testing and the surveyor's periodic full-load verification are not substitutes for each other.
