extensions.text: Because the emergency generator's entire value depends on cold, unattended, first-time-right starting per the dead-ship starting principle this node describes, its maintenance priorities differ from a normally-running engine's. Starting batteries: the single highest-impact maintenance item -- kept on continuous trickle/float charge, with specific gravity (for flooded lead-acid) or terminal voltage checked on a fixed schedule, since a battery bank that reads healthy at rest can still fail to deliver the high starting current required (see this object's failure-modes record on sulfation). Fuel system: the fuel day tank must be kept topped up and the fuel itself rotated or treated, since a set that sits idle between tests is exactly where stale fuel, water contamination, and air locks in the fuel line accumulate unnoticed -- these are documented as the leading cause of a generator that cranks but fails to actually fire on demand. Cooling and lubrication: jacket-water heaters (where fitted) keep the engine at a ready-to-start temperature; lubricating oil level and condition still need scheduled checks despite the engine running only briefly each week. Governor and safety shutdown circuits: overspeed, low-lube-oil-pressure, and high-jacket-water-temperature trips must be tested to confirm they protect the set without being so sensitive they cause nuisance shutdowns during an actual emergency start -- a shutdown circuit that is itself unreliable defeats the regulation's purpose as surely as a set that won't start at all.

extensions.text: Three documented failure categories for emergency generators, each pointing to a different corrective action rather than a single generic 'generator failed to start': battery/starting-energy failure -- most commonly sulfation of lead-acid starting batteries from long periods of float-charge without a real discharge cycle, which reduces effective capacity so the battery reads a healthy resting voltage but cannot deliver the sustained high current a diesel start demands; this is the single most common documented cause of a failed emergency-generator start. Fuel-system failure -- most commonly stale or water-contaminated fuel and air trapped in the fuel line from a set that sits idle between tests, causing an engine that cranks vigorously (batteries fine) but never actually fires; this is the most common cause of a startup failure specifically, as distinct from a no-crank failure. Control/safety-circuit failure -- the engine is mechanically capable of starting and running, but a sensor or safety shutdown circuit (overspeed, low lube-oil pressure, high jacket-water temperature) trips the set immediately after starting, or a faulty sensor prevents the automatic-start signal from reaching the engine at all; because these three categories require different responses -- battery replacement/equalising charge, fuel system draining and bleeding, versus sensor/shutdown-circuit diagnosis -- distinguishing which one occurred during an actual test or casualty matters more than simply logging 'generator failed'. A documented, genuine ISM-audit scenario (MIW QB1_supplementary.html -- see this object's qb-reference record) illustrates a related but distinct failure mode: a leaking emergency generator fuel valve discovered during an audit, framed as a 'trap question' testing whether the candidate recognises it as a non-conformity requiring correction rather than a minor housekeeping item, since a leaking fuel valve on this specific machine directly threatens the very readiness Reg 42 exists to guarantee.

extensions.text: Structured decision rule for reasoning about emergency generator compliance, distilled from this node's other records rather than independently authored. To assess whether an emergency source of electrical power satisfies the regime as currently understood from evidence gathered in this pass, check in order: (1) STARTING CAPABILITY -- can the set self-start from cold (0 degrees C) without any external electrical supply, and does it actually reach rated speed/voltage/frequency and connect to the emergency switchboard within 45 seconds of main power loss, per SOLAS II-1/42.3? A set that starts but connects slower than 45 seconds fails regardless of any other factor. (2) TRANSITIONAL COVERAGE -- is a transitional battery source in place and charged, bridging the 45-second gap so essential lighting/communications never actually go dark? (3) LOAD SCHEDULE -- can the set carry the full named consumer list (navigation lights, GMDSS, internal communications, fire detection/alarm, fire pump, sprinkler pump, emergency bilge pump, steering gear) for 36 hours on a passenger ship or 18 hours on a cargo ship, per Reg 42.2? (4) OPERABILITY UNDER CASUALTY CONDITIONS -- does the set, prime mover and switchboard remain functional at up to 22.5 degrees list and 10 degrees trim, per Reg 42.7 -- not just upright? (5) TESTING DISCIPLINE -- are weekly no-load starts, monthly automatic-changeover tests, and quarterly/annual full blackout load tests actually logged with elapsed start time recorded, not just pass/fail? extensions.text: A lifeboat is a certified assembly, not a single approved item -- LSA Code 4.4 requires an approval plate and conformity certificate recording manufacturer, model, capacity and hull material for the boat as a whole, and each major subsystem is separately engineered. Hull and structure: a rigid, self-righting-capable hull that must remain positively stable in calm water even when swamped and open to the sea, and survive a 3.0 m drop test into the water undamaged (LSA Code 4.4.1). Propulsion: a compression-ignition engine capable of cold-starting at -15 degrees C within 2 minutes, with 24 hours of fuel at 6 knots fully loaded and towing capability at 5 knots (LSA Code 4.4.6). Release system: the on-load/off-load release hook -- engineered separately enough that this repository models it as its own Engineering Object (see offload-release-hook) -- fitted with a mechanical hydrostatic interlock, dual colour-coded reset indicators, and a factor of safety of at least 6 on both the mechanism and the painter (LSA Code 4.4.7). Enclosure (totally enclosed variants): a rigid watertight canopy with hatches operable from inside and outside, capable of supporting the fully loaded boat capsized, and self-righting when fully or partially loaded, with occupants secured by contrasting-colour safety belts (LSA Code 4.6.1). Air support system (where fitted): supplies breathable air for at least 10 minutes with engine running, holding cabin pressure within 20 hPa of ambient (LSA Code 4.6.3). Launching interface: falls, davit and painter connecting the boat to its dedicated launching appliance -- modelled separately in this repository as the lifeboat-davit and launching-appliance Engineering Objects, since the appliance itself is a distinct piece of certified equipment from the boat it launches.

extensions.text: LSA Code 4.4's requirements only make sense read against the casualty they exist to survive: a lifeboat is specified for the worst-case abandon-ship scenario, not the average one. The 3.0 m drop test (4.4.1) exists because a real launch may not go cleanly -- a jammed davit or a heavy sea can mean the boat enters the water from height, and the hull must survive that undamaged with occupants aboard. The -15 degrees C/2-minute cold-start requirement (4.4.6) reflects that the casualty triggering abandonment could itself be in cold-climate operation, precisely when a normal engine is hardest to start and least forgivable to fail. This repository deliberately models three parts of the wider lifeboat system as separate Engineering Objects rather than folding them into this one: the on-load/off-load release hook (offload-release-hook), because its own engineering -- hydrostatic interlock, dual reset indicators, factor of safety 6 -- and its own documented accident history are substantial enough to warrant independent treatment, not because it is unrelated; and the davit/launching appliance (lifeboat-davit, launching-appliance), because SOLAS and LSA Code regulate the launching apparatus as a distinct piece of certified equipment from the boat it launches, and a lifeboat's own compliance record says nothing about whether the davit lowering it is itself compliant. Free-fall lifeboats (LSA Code 4.7) are a genuine engineering variant, not just a launching method: they build on the totally-enclosed requirements of 4.6 but add drop-height structural margin (1.3x certification height), positive-headway-after-launch performance, and a release system operable only from inside the boat -- because a free-fall launch has no external operator to abort or adjust it once initiated, unlike a davit-lowered boat.

extensions.text: Lifeboat drill discipline runs on an escalating cadence, each tier proving a different thing: weekly, a visual inspection under the supervision of a senior officer confirms general readiness -- boat, falls, and release gear look correct and the on-load release gear is properly reset, without launching. Monthly, every lifeboat is turned out from its stowed position (weather permitting) and the condition of the life-saving equipment aboard is checked -- proving the boat actually moves on its falls, not just that it looks ready. Every 3 months (SOLAS III/19.3, the node this record is attached to), each lifeboat must actually be launched and manoeuvred in the water by its assigned operating crew -- the first tier that proves the complete chain (davit, falls, release gear, engine, steering) works together, not just in isolation. Free-fall lifeboats follow a separate, less frequent cadence for the full launch itself: SOLAS III/19.4 permits a simulated (non-launching) drill at the normal monthly/quarterly cadence, but requires an actual free-fall launch with only the required operating crew on board at least once every 6 months -- deliberately less frequent than a davit-launched boat's quarterly wet drill, because a free-fall launch is a one-way, higher-consequence event that cannot be aborted partway through once initiated.

extensions.text: The release mechanism is the single most heavily survey-scrutinised part of the lifeboat system, for documented safety reasons (see this object's failure-modes and regulatory-lineage records). A survey/inspection of the release gear checks, in order: (1) reset confirmation -- both colour-coded reset indicators must show the hook is genuinely reset, not just visually appear closed, since a hook that looks reset but isn't is exactly the failure mode the dual-indicator requirement exists to catch; (2) hydrostatic interlock function -- verified as part of the periodic thorough examination, confirming the interlock still prevents on-load release above the design height rather than releasing intermittently or prematurely; (3) five-yearly thorough examination and overhaul by the manufacturer's representative or an approved service provider, as required for on-load release gear generally, including a proof-load test at 1.1 times the weight of the fully equipped, fully loaded survival craft; (4) wear on the cam/hook engagement faces -- a documented degradation mode that reduces the margin before unintended release, checked visually and by the manufacturer's tolerance specification, not just by confirming the hook currently holds; (5) painter and structural attachment points, against the same factor-of-safety-6 standard applied to the release mechanism itself. A hook that passes a routine reset check is not the same as a hook that has passed its 5-yearly thorough examination -- the two are complementary, not substitutes for each other, and PSC/flag inspectors specifically check for the latter's documentation, not just the former's appearance.

extensions.text: Lifeboat maintenance layers across several timescales, each catching a different degradation mode. Weekly: visual inspection of the boat, falls and release gear condition under a senior officer's supervision -- catching obvious deterioration (corrosion, chafing, damaged canopy) before it becomes a functional failure. Monthly: turning the boat out from its stowed position and running the engine, proving the propulsion and launching path are not merely present but actually functional -- a boat that hasn't moved on its falls in months is the point at which stiction, corrosion of moving parts, or a seized engine first goes undetected. Annual: a thorough examination by a competent person covering structure, engine, release gear and ventilation/air-support systems -- the first tier deep enough to catch internal degradation invisible to a weekly walk-past. Five-yearly: davit falls (wires) must be turned end-for-end or replaced outright, regardless of what visual inspection shows, because internal wire corrosion is invisible externally and progressively reduces breaking strength -- this is a hard calendar requirement, not a condition-based one, precisely because the failure mode it guards against cannot be reliably caught by inspection alone. The release gear itself receives its own five-yearly thorough examination and proof-load test (see this object's inspection-guidance record) on the same non-negotiable calendar logic. Fuel system: because the engine may sit unstarted for weeks between tests, fuel quality (water contamination, microbial growth, wax formation in cold storage) degrades exactly where it will not be noticed until the one moment reliability matters -- fuel rotation/quality checks belong on the same maintenance calendar as the engine test itself, not as an afterthought.

extensions.text: Two distinct, well-documented failure categories account for most serious lifeboat casualties, and they demand different corrective responses -- treating both as generic 'lifeboat accidents' obscures which fix actually applies. Release-hook premature or uncontrolled release: historically the single most common cause of fatal lifeboat casualties industry-wide, most often from cam-to-horn engagement wear, a hydrostatic interlock that fails to hold reliably, or crew resetting the hook incorrectly after a drill -- the boat drops from height (davit height, not the intended near-water release point) with occupants aboard. This pattern, repeated across many vessels and operators rather than a single incident, is what drove the regulatory response described in this object's regulatory-lineage record. Falls/davit-wire failure: a structurally separate failure mode where the hoisting wire itself parts, typically from fatigue or internal corrosion invisible on external inspection -- the documented 2013 Thomson Majesty casualty (five crew fatalities during a drill at La Palma, Canary Islands) is attributed to a hoisting-wire failure on one side of the davit, which threw the full dynamic load onto the remaining wire and caused it to part as well, not to a release-hook fault. These two categories point to different maintenance responses: hook wear is caught by the release-gear's own inspection/overhaul regime (see this object's inspection-guidance record), while wire fatigue is why falls replacement is a hard five-year calendar requirement regardless of visual condition (see this object's maintenance-guidance record) -- neither substitutes for the other.

extensions.text: IMO Resolution MSC.320(89) amended LSA Code Chapter IV's on-load release and retrieval system requirements (the 4.4.7.6.4-4.4.7.6.6 sub-paragraphs this node's 4.4.7.6 citation covers), applying to ships constructed on or after 1 July 2014. Separately, SOLAS Regulation III/1.5 (entered into force 1 January 2013) required Administrations to evaluate EXISTING on-load release hooks against the same amended standard and replace any found non-compliant -- driven by a documented pattern of fatal and injury casualties during lifeboat drills traced to premature or uncontrolled release-hook failures (see this object's failure-modes record), not by a single incident. IMO Resolution MSC.1/Circ.1392 (27 May 2011) provides the step-by-step guidelines flag states, shipowners and manufacturers use to carry out that evaluation. The retrofit compliance timeline for existing ships: a manufacturer's Factual Statement (compliant hooks already examined) or a flag-State Statement of Acceptance was required after the vessel's next scheduled dry-docking, with a hard deadline of 1 July 2019 regardless of drydocking schedule. This is a safety-driven retrofit mandate specifically targeting the release mechanism -- it does not alter the underlying structural/performance standards (3.0 m drop test, -15 degrees C cold start, 6-knot speed) this repository's other lifeboat nodes already describe, which predate MSC.320(89) and were not reopened by it. No amendment specifically to the LSA Code 4.4.1 drop-test standard or the 4.4.6 propulsion standard was found in this research pass (2026-07-25) -- stated as a checked finding, not an unchecked assumption.

extensions.text: Structured decision rule for reasoning about lifeboat compliance, distilled from this node's other records rather than independently authored. To assess whether a lifeboat arrangement satisfies the regime as currently understood from evidence gathered in this pass, check in order: (1) STRUCTURAL INTEGRITY -- is the hull rigid, self-righting-capable, and drop-test certified to at least 3.0 m (LSA Code 4.4.1)? (2) PROPULSION -- does the engine cold-start at -15 degrees C within 2 minutes, and does the fuel capacity support 24 hours at 6 knots fully loaded (LSA Code 4.4.6)? (3) RELEASE SYSTEM -- is the on-load/off-load release mechanism fitted with a functioning hydrostatic interlock, dual reset indicators, and a verified factor of safety of at least 6, with its own 5-yearly thorough examination current? This is the single highest-consequence check -- release-hook failure is the most common cause of fatal lifeboat casualties historically, so a 'yes' elsewhere cannot offset a 'no' here. (4) ENCLOSURE (totally enclosed variants) -- is the canopy watertight, self-righting when loaded, and (if air-support-equipped) capable of at least 10 minutes' breathable air within 20 hPa cabin overpressure? (5) DRILL DISCIPLINE -- is the 3-monthly wet launch (or 6-monthly free-fall launch, for free-fall variants) actually logged, not just the weekly/monthly non-launching checks? A single 'no' on checks 1-3 is sufficient to flag the arrangement for engineering review regardless of the others, since each maps to a distinct, independently documented failure category (structural, propulsion, release) rather than a weighted score. One structural caveat distilled from this pass's engineering-context and regulatory-lineage records: this repository does not yet model SOLAS III/1.5 (the existing-ship release-hook retrofit mandate) or SOLAS III Reg 20 (LSA maintenance/inspection requirements) as nodes -- any reasoning about a specific vessel's retrofit compliance status should be treated as unverified against this repository until those gaps are closed. extensions.text: The oily water separator (OWS) is a treatment train, not a single filter, and MARPOL Annex I Regulation 14 regulates the whole train together with the equipment it feeds. Primary (gravity) stage: a coalescer/gravity separator that removes free, non-emulsified oil by density difference -- the stage every approved unit has had since the original 1992 standard. Secondary (emulsion-breaking) stage: ultrafiltration, flocculation or carbon adsorption that breaks stable oil-in-water emulsions created by detergents, surfactants and scavenge soot -- mandatory under the current standard (see this object's regulatory-lineage record) but absent from older units, which is exactly why a modern unit can pass clean test water yet fail on real bilge water (see this object's failure-modes record). Oil Content Meter / Oil Discharge Monitor (OCM/ODM): a dedicated sensor, fixed on a vertical section of pipe immediately before the overboard valve, continuously measuring the treated effluent's oil content in ppm. Alarm and automatic stopping device: mandatory on ships of 10,000 GT and above (MARPOL Annex I Reg 14.2) -- the alarm trips and a 3-way valve automatically diverts discharge back to the bilge holding tank the instant the OCM reads above 15 ppm, so the system fails safe rather than relying on a crew member noticing an alarm. Sludge tank and standard discharge connection: the separated oil residue does not vanish -- it is routed to a dedicated sludge tank (MARPOL Annex I Reg 12), piped so it has no direct connection to the bilge discharge line, and offloaded ashore through a standardised flange (Reg 13) sized 215 mm outer diameter with a 183 mm bolt circle -- this piping separation is the physical basis for detecting an unauthorised bypass ('magic pipe') arrangement.

extensions.text: The 15 ppm limit and the 10,000 GT auto-stop threshold in Regulation 14 only make engineering sense read alongside Regulation 15's operational discharge criteria and Regulation 12's sludge-tank requirement, which this repository models as separate but directly linked nodes. Regulation 14 answers 'what equipment must be fitted'; Regulation 15 answers 'under what conditions may it actually discharge' (en route, outside special areas, not from cargo pump-room bilges); Regulation 12 answers 'where does the removed oil go' -- the separator does not destroy oil, it concentrates it into sludge that still needs safe onward disposal, which is why sludge-tank piping isolation (Reg 12.2) is as much a part of pollution-prevention engineering as the separator itself. The 10,000 GT threshold for mandatory automatic stopping (Reg 14.2) reflects a practical judgement: below that size, the volume of bilge water processed and the consequence of an undetected excursion above 15 ppm is smaller, so a simple alarm relying on crew response was judged adequate; above it, the automatic 3-way stopping device removes the human-response step entirely. This repository does not yet model MARPOL Annex I Regulation 15, paragraph 4 (the Antarctic Area's complete discharge prohibition, distinct from and stricter than the general special-area conditions in the Reg 15.2 node this object already references) as its own node -- see this object's oral-notes-reference record for the distinction, verified independently via web research rather than assumed from the existing 15.2 summary's mention of 'Antarctic area' among the named special areas.

extensions.text: Every OWS operation -- start, stop, discharge, recirculation-to-bilge, and any transfer of bilge water or sludge -- must be entered chronologically in the Oil Record Book Part I, signed by the responsible officer and countersigned by the master, and retained on board for at least three years. This is not paperwork bolted on after the fact: it is the primary document a Port State Control officer cross-checks against the equipment itself, and a mismatch between what the ORB claims and what the equipment's own data shows (electronic OCM log, tank soundings, bunker/sludge landing receipts) is treated as a serious finding regardless of whether an actual illegal discharge is proven, because a falsified or incomplete ORB is itself a MARPOL offence. Practical discipline: log the actual event as it happens, not from memory at watch changeover; record sludge tank soundings before and after a landing/incineration/transfer so quantities reconcile; and treat any OCM alarm or automatic stop event as an ORB entry in its own right, not just an equipment log entry -- an alarm that triggered but was never logged is exactly the kind of gap PSC and flag-state audits are trained to look for.

extensions.text: This node's own requirement -- that sludge piping has no direct connection to bilge discharge piping and no overboard connection other than the standard discharge connection -- is the physical basis PSC and flag-state surveyors use to detect an unauthorised bypass ('magic pipe') arrangement. A documented, genuine PSC scenario (see this object's oral-notes-reference record): an officer notices heavy black oil residue in the OWS overboard sight-glass despite the Oil Record Book showing all recent discharges under 15 ppm -- the correct response is to isolate and lock out the overboard line immediately (demonstrating good faith and stopping any ongoing non-compliant discharge), not to argue the ORB figures first. A survey/inspection checks, in order: (1) physical piping trace -- does the sludge/bilge piping run exactly as the approved drawings show, with no unauthorised valve, flexible hose, or flange that could route bilge water around the OWS/OCM entirely; (2) OCM sampling-point integrity -- is the sample line free of leaks, air bubbles, or scale that would cause a false-clean reading rather than an accurate one; (3) 3-way valve function -- does the automatic stopping/recirculation device actually divert flow when commanded, tested with a certified test fluid, not just observed to be present; (4) OCM calibration currency -- checked at IOPP Certificate renewal and against the ±5 ppm accuracy tolerance IMO guidance requires; (5) ORB cross-check -- do logged operations, sludge tank soundings, and any landing receipts reconcile with each other, not just with the equipment's own internal log. A unit that reads clean on a calibration test but has never been checked against real, contaminated bilge water has only been proven to work on water it was never actually designed to struggle with.

extensions.text: OWS maintenance runs on a similar escalating calendar to other pollution-prevention equipment, tuned to what each check can actually catch. Weekly: inspect for leaks, blockages and visible component wear, and confirm electrical connections and sensor functions are intact -- catching obvious degradation before it becomes a functional failure. Monthly: clean the oil sensor electrode (a common source of drifting false readings if left fouled), carry out an internal visual inspection of the overboard pipe, test the 3-way stopping/recirculation valve's operation, and verify seals are properly fitted. Coalescer/filter elements: typical service life is 1-2 years under normal duty, but the element should be cleaned or inspected at least annually regardless, since a partially fouled coalescer degrades gradually rather than failing outright -- a unit that 'still works' on a quick visual check can already be passing more oil than its rated performance. OCM (Oil Content Meter) calibration: recalibrate at least every 12 months, or per the manufacturer's own interval if shorter, and specifically re-verify accuracy at IOPP Certificate renewal -- IMO guidance requires the alarm to remain accurate within plus-or-minus 5 ppm, a tolerance that erodes with sensor lens fouling or scaling over time even without any single dramatic failure event.

extensions.text: Two distinct, well-documented failure categories account for most OWS non-compliance findings, and -- as with this repository's other equipment nodes -- they demand different diagnoses rather than a single generic 'OWS failed'. Genuine treatment failure: the unit correctly passes clean test water (proving the OCM sensor itself is calibrated) but fails on actual bilge water because it cannot break stable oil-in-water emulsions created by detergents, surfactants and scavenge soot -- a documented, genuine MIW oral-exam scenario frames this precisely: 'OWS passes clean water but fails on bilge water -- troubleshoot', with the correct diagnosis being emulsion-breaking failure (fouled or exhausted secondary-stage coalescer/filter elements, or active chemical cleaning contaminating the bilge well), not sensor calibration. Deliberate bypass ('magic pipe'): an unauthorised piping arrangement routes bilge water around the OWS/OCM entirely, discharging untreated -- this is fraud, not an equipment fault, and is why MARPOL Annex I Reg 12.2's piping-isolation requirement (see this object's inspection-guidance record) exists as a physical, inspectable control rather than relying on the OCM reading alone. A third, narrower failure mode sits between these two: OCM sensor fouling or optical-cell scaling causing a false-clean reading even though the water passing through is not actually clean -- distinguishable from a genuine treatment failure because the equipment itself is malfunctioning rather than merely under-capable, and from a bypass because the water genuinely did pass through the sensor, just inaccurately measured. Distinguishing which of these three occurred matters directly for the corrective action: emulsion-breaking failure is fixed by servicing/replacing the secondary treatment stage; sensor fouling is fixed by cleaning/recalibrating the OCM; a bypass is a compliance and disciplinary matter, not a maintenance one.

extensions.text: IMO Resolution MEPC.60(33), adopted 30 October 1992, was the original type-approval standard for oil filtering equipment -- gravity/coalescer separation only, unable to reliably break stable oil-in-water emulsions. IMO Resolution MEPC.107(49), adopted 18 July 2003, superseded it with a substantially stricter standard: a mandatory secondary emulsion-breaking stage, a tamper-resistant 15 ppm alarm with mandatory automatic stopping and closed-loop recirculation, a fast sensor response (on the order of 5 seconds) and bounded total control-loop time (on the order of 20 seconds) verified during type-approval slug testing, a fixed OCM sampling point immediately before the overboard valve, and a mandatory internal electronic log (date/time/alarm status/valve position) retained securely for at least 18 months. MEPC.107(49) became the applicable standard for equipment installed on or after 1 January 2005, and is incorporated into MARPOL Annex I Regulation 14 as revised (that revised Annex I entered into force 1 January 2007) -- this node's own citation to MEPC.107(49) reflects that incorporation. Existing MEPC.60(33)-compliant units already in service were not automatically rendered illegal: IMO Resolution MEPC.205(62) (adopted 15 July 2011) provides guidelines and specifications for add-on equipment that upgrades an existing MEPC.60(33) unit to meet MEPC.107(49)-equivalent performance, an alternative to full replacement. No amendment specifically altering the 15 ppm concentration limit itself, or the 10,000 GT automatic-stopping threshold in Reg 14.2, was found in this research pass (2026-07-25) -- stated as a checked finding, not an unchecked assumption, per the discipline already applied to this repository's other regulatory-lineage records.

extensions.text: Structured decision rule for reasoning about OWS compliance, distilled from this node's other records rather than independently authored. To assess whether an oily water separator arrangement satisfies the regime as currently understood from evidence gathered in this pass, check in order: (1) EQUIPMENT STANDARD -- is the fitted unit approved to MEPC.107(49) (mandatory for equipment installed on or after 2005-01-01), or is it an older MEPC.60(33) unit with a documented MEPC.205(62) add-on upgrade -- an unmodified pre-2003 unit with no upgrade is the highest-risk configuration for genuine emulsion-breaking failure. (2) AUTOMATIC PROTECTION -- for ships of 10,000 GT and above, is the automatic 15 ppm alarm and 3-way stopping/recirculation device actually fitted and functional, not merely present (Reg 14.2)? (3) PIPING INTEGRITY -- does the sludge/bilge piping run exactly as approved, with no unauthorised bypass connection around the OWS/OCM (Reg 12.2) -- this is a compliance and fraud check, not a maintenance one, and a single 'no' here overrides everything else regardless of how well the equipment itself performs. (4) DOCUMENTATION -- does the Oil Record Book Part I reconcile with the equipment's own electronic log, sludge tank soundings, and any landing receipts (Reg 17)? (5) DISCHARGE CONDITIONS -- is the vessel actually en route, outside a special area (or meeting the stricter special-area conditions), and not discharging from cargo pump-room bilges, when any discharge occurs (Reg 15)? A single 'no' on checks 1-3 is sufficient to flag the arrangement for engineering or compliance review regardless of the others, since each maps to a distinct, independently documented failure or fraud category (equipment capability, automatic protection, physical bypass) rather than a weighted score. One structural caveat distilled from this pass's engineering-context record: this repository does not yet model MARPOL Annex I Reg 15, paragraph 4 (the Antarctic Area's complete discharge prohibition) as its own node -- any reasoning about Antarctic-area-specific compliance should be treated as unverified against this repository until that gap is closed. This rule reflects only what was verified in this authoring pass (2026-07-25) and should be re-validated against the current regulation text before being relied on for an actual compliance determination.
